summary.title: What Is CAP Theorem?
summary.one_liner: The CAP theorem says a distributed data system can guarantee at most two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance when a network partition occurs, and this page explains why and how real systems trade these off.
takeaways: During a network partition you must choose between consistency and availability; partition tolerance is treated as a baseline rather than an optional choice.
CP systems block or reject some operations during partitions to keep data consistent, while AP systems keep serving requests and reconcile divergent data later.
Eventual consistency, tunable consistency levels and quorum reads/writes are common ways real systems work around the strict CAP trade-off.
The theorem is closely tied to safety and liveness properties and to the FLP impossibility result on consensus, per the author's view.
summary.summary: This Quora page collects several answers to the question of what the CAP theorem is, with the top answer written by an author who explains it through a two-node replicated system and the C-versus-A trade-off under partitions. Other sections cover the asynchronous-network formulation of the theorem (citing Gilbert and Lynch style definitions), the FLP connection, and examples such as DynamoDB's eventual consistency. Later answers give shorter definitions, list CP and AP example databases (HBase, ZooKeeper, etcd, Cassandra, Riak, Spanner), and add practical design notes on quorums, SLAs and hybrid architectures. Note that the page is a multi-answer Q&A thread rather than a single article, and some answers carry the same text repeated.
